To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the numbers of cells in each type of neurosecretory cell change during the final molting process in a predictable manner.

1) the number of neurosecretory cells in the brain of R. prolixus is reduced by 50% during the final molting stage; 2) neurosecretory cells are not replaced by new cells in the brain, and 3) neurosecretory cell number is restored to normal after molting.
the neurosecretory cell types are not all equally sensitive to molting hormone and that the neurosecretary cells are not all equally responsive to molting hormone.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the study of the neurosecretion of the insect brain, its development and its relation to the endocrine control of molting and metamorphosis.
the dynamics of neurosecretion in insects and the role of neurosecretion as an endocrine system.
the study of insect growth and development and the role of the neurosecretion in this process.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

there are five cell types, which are not necessarily identical to the five cell types described by others, but are similar in number and distribution to those reported for the neurosecretory cells in other insects.
in the final molt of R. prolixus, the neurosecretory cells undergo a sequence of changes that are consistent with the hypothesis that they are involved in the regulation of molting and ecdysis.

the neurosecretory cells are involved in the control of the molting process, and the neurohormone(s) they secrete is/are probably responsible for the synthesis of the molting hormone, and the release of it into the hemolymph.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

we have demonstrated that the brain of Rhodniu sprolixus contains five types of neurosecretory cells, that they are distributed among three nuclei, that their numbers are constant throughout the life of the insect, and that the cells are involved in molting, reproduction and the regulation of water balance.
the neuroendocrine system of the insect brain is a highly complex system that regulates the molting cycle and other aspects of growth, development, and reproduction.
we are trying to understand how a cell can change its shape and how it can change its size, and how it can do that in an organized manner.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the neurosecretory cells in the brain of the blood-sucking bug, Rhodniu prolixus, are very sensitive to the nutritional status of the animal and to molting.
the neurosecretory cells of the insect brain are not static but change in number during growth and molts.
the neurosecretory neurons are not a homogenous population.
